record.title: He, she, it + -s
record.rule: In the present simple, add -s or -es to the verb after he, she, it or one person or thing: she sings, he fixes, the dog barks.
record.examples: My aunt teaches music. | It rains a lot in July.
record.tip: I, you, we, they: no -s (they play).
record.check_question: Choose: She ___ to music every evening.
record.evidence_status: teaching content; status candidate: written by OpenPath for the first web version; not yet reviewed by educators; educator review: none

record.title: Plural subjects
record.rule: A plural subject takes a plural verb: the mice run, the trees grow, my cousins live nearby.
record.examples: The birds are on the roof. | These shoes look new.
record.tip: Find the subject first, then match the verb to it.
record.evidence_status: teaching content; status candidate: written by OpenPath for the first web version; not yet reviewed by educators; educator review: none

record.title: Two subjects with and
record.rule: Two subjects joined by and take a plural verb: Anil and Sara are friends.
record.examples: My sister and I walk to school. | Bread and butter is…
record.tip: and adds the subjects together, so the verb is plural.
record.check_question: Choose: Tom and his dog ___ in the park.
record.check_explanation: Tom and his dog = two: are.
record.evidence_status: teaching content; status candidate: written by OpenPath for the first web version; not yet reviewed by educators; educator review: none

record.title: Words between subject and verb
record.rule: The verb agrees with the subject, not with a noun just before it: The jar of sweets is empty. The cup of tea is hot.
record.examples: The colour of the flowers is bright. | The boys in the team are tired.
record.tip: Cover the words between: 'The box … is'.
record.check_question: Choose: The basket of eggs ___ full.
record.check_explanation: The subject is the basket (one): is.
record.evidence_status: teaching content; status candidate: written by OpenPath for the first web version; not yet reviewed by educators; educator review: none

record.title: Each, every, everyone
record.rule: each, every, everyone, nobody and somebody take a singular verb: Each of the girls has a ticket. Everyone is here.
record.examples: Every child needs sleep. | Somebody is at the door.
record.tip: Each of the… is still one at a time: singular.
record.check_question: Choose: Each of the players ___ a shirt.
record.evidence_status: teaching content; status candidate: written by OpenPath for the first web version; not yet reviewed by educators; educator review: none

record.title: either … or, neither … nor
record.rule: With either … or and neither … nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: Neither the driver nor the passengers were hurt. Either the girls or their father is coming.
record.examples: Either my parents or my aunt is coming. | Neither the dog nor the cats were hungry.
record.tip: Look at the subject closest to the verb.
record.check_question: Choose: Neither Priya nor her brothers ___ at home.
record.check_explanation: The nearer subject, brothers, is plural: are.
record.evidence_status: teaching content; status candidate: written by OpenPath for the first web version; not yet reviewed by educators; educator review: none

record.title: Inverted order; a number of
record.rule: When the verb comes first, find the subject after it: There are many birds. Here comes the bus. 'A number of' is plural; 'the number of' is singular.
record.examples: A number of shops were closed. | The number of cars is growing.
record.tip: Turn the sentence round: many birds are there.
record.check_question: Choose: There ___ three books on the desk.
record.check_explanation: The subject is three books: are.
record.evidence_status: teaching content; status candidate: written by OpenPath for the first web version; not yet reviewed by educators; educator review: none

record.title: Present simple and regular past
record.rule: Use the present simple for habits and facts (I walk to school), and add -ed for most past actions (Yesterday I walked).
record.examples: Every day she plays cricket. | Last week we visited Amma.
record.tip: Time words help: every day → present; yesterday, last week → past.
record.check_question: Choose the right verb: Yesterday we ___ to the park.
record.check_options: A. walk | B. walked | C. walks
record.check_explanation: Yesterday tells you it is the past: walked.
record.evidence_status: teaching content; status candidate: written by OpenPath for the first web version; not yet reviewed by educators; educator review: none

record.title: Common irregular past forms
record.rule: Many common verbs do not take -ed in the past: go → went, buy → bought, see → saw, eat → ate.
record.examples: We went to the market and bought mangoes. | I saw a film and ate popcorn.
record.tip: Learn these by heart; never write goed or buyed.
record.check_question: Choose the right verb: She ___ a new bag last week.
record.check_options: A. buyed | B. bought | C. buy
record.evidence_status: teaching content; status candidate: written by OpenPath for the first web version; not yet reviewed by educators; educator review: none

record.title: Questions and negatives with did
record.rule: After did and didn't, use the base form of the verb: Did you go? I didn't see it. (Not: Did you went?)
record.examples: Did she finish her homework? | We didn't watch TV.
record.tip: did already shows the past, so the verb stays in its base form.
record.check_options: A. saw | B. see | C. seen
record.check_explanation: After did, use the base form: see.
record.evidence_status: teaching content; status candidate: written by OpenPath for the first web version; not yet reviewed by educators; educator review: none

record.title: Keeping the tense steady
record.rule: When you tell a story in the past, keep it in the past: She opened the door and saw a dog. Learn less common irregular forms: catch → caught, choose → chose, lead → led.
record.examples: He caught the ball and threw it back. | They chose a leader who led them well.
record.tip: Read your sentences again and check every verb is in the same time.
record.check_question: Choose: The team ___ the cup last year.
record.check_options: A. win | B. won | C. wins
record.check_explanation: last year is the past: won.
record.evidence_status: teaching content; status candidate: written by OpenPath for the first web version; not yet reviewed by educators; educator review: none

record.title: Uncommon irregular forms
record.rule: Some irregular verbs are rare but appear in books: seek → sought, weep → wept, forbid → forbade, bear → bore.
record.examples: They sought help from the teacher. | She wept with joy.
record.tip: If you are unsure, check a dictionary: it lists irregular past forms.

record.title: a or an
record.rule: Use an before a word that starts with a vowel (a, e, i, o, u) and a before a consonant: an orange, an egg, a ball, a cat.
record.examples: an inkpot, an onion | a pencil, a dog
record.tip: Say it aloud: 'an apple' is easier to say than 'a apple'.
record.check_explanation: egg starts with a vowel: an egg.

record.title: a first, then the
record.rule: Use a when you first mention something, then the when you mention it again: I found a shell. The shell was pink. Use a before a job: He is a farmer.
record.examples: We bought a kite. The kite was red. | My uncle is a doctor.
record.tip: a = one of many; the = the one we both know about.
record.check_explanation: Use a or an before a job: an engineer.

record.title: a or an by sound
